title: Ponderosa Park Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Ponderosa Park wells have a 360-foot median depth and typical completed costs of $24,000-$37,200.
h1: Ponderosa Park, Colorado Well and Drilling Guide
intro_html:
Buying land in Ponderosa Park means understanding the Denver Basin well records before you rely on a contractor’s estimate or a seller’s water claims. Nearby permitted wells have a 360-foot median depth, with most falling between 300 and 434 feet. Reported production is generally useful for a household, but the records do not tell the whole story about water quality, legal use, storage, septic suitability, or the cost of reaching a building site.

This page covers permitted wells within five miles of Ponderosa Park, including local depth, yield, water-level, permit, driller, cost, and environmental information. Use it to screen a property, then confirm the specific permit, well construction, water rights, and site conditions before closing or starting construction.

sections.heading: Ponderosa Park wells are usually deep Denver Basin wells
sections.html:
The local depth data point to a substantial drilling project rather than a shallow well. The median completed depth is 360 feet, and the middle half of reported wells runs from 300 to 434 feet. About 65% of wells are between 300 and 600 feet, while 11% exceed 600 feet. The deepest recorded well reaches 2,318 feet.

All mapped wells are identified with Denver Basin aquifers. The Upper Dawson appears on 2,384 permits, an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer on 1,795, and the Lower Dawson on 752. Those formations can vary substantially across a property. For a drilling bid, use the local median as a planning reference, not a guarantee. Access, casing, grout, geology, and the target aquifer can move the final depth well beyond a simple per-foot estimate.

sections.heading: What a Ponderosa Park well is likely to produce
sections.html:
Among wells with reported pump yields, the median is 13.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. That is a reasonably strong local production pattern for a household well, although a pump test and the well’s permit conditions matter more than a regional median when evaluating a particular lot.

The yield mix is also encouraging: 72% of reported wells produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 27% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Only 1% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, with no reported wells under 1 gallon per minute in this dataset. A high yield does not automatically mean unrestricted use. Many permits are domestic or household permits, and an exempt household-use well remains subject to its permitted uses and Colorado water law.

sections.heading: Water levels in Ponderosa Park need property-level checking
sections.html:
Reported static water levels have a median depth of 180 feet below ground, with the middle half between 125 and 245 feet. That affects pump setting, electrical planning, storage, and the amount of water a driller must lift. Static level is not the same as pumping level, so a buyer should request the well construction report and any available pump-test information.

The decade series does not show a simple, continuous decline. Median depth to water was 144 feet in the 1970s, 164 in the 1980s, 230 in the 1990s, 215 in the 2000s, 170 in the 2010s, and 200 in the 2020s. Measurements come from different wells and years, so this is regional context rather than proof of a changing water table at your parcel.

sections.heading: Permit history and drillers around Ponderosa Park
sections.html:
The records show the heaviest permit activity from the 1970s through the 1990s: 972 permits in the 1970s, 1,172 in the 1980s, and 1,641 in the 1990s. Activity was lower in later decades, with 666 permits in the 2000s, 372 in the 2010s, and 296 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most active names in these records are Hamacher Well Works Inc (Hamacher, Alan Ray) with 1,046 records, Hier Drilling Co Inc (Hier, Bruce A.) with 853, and Hier Drilling Co. (Hier, Peter J) with 728. These counts describe permit records, not current availability, pricing, or a quality ranking. Verify licensing, insurance, references, and the proposed scope directly before hiring.

sections.heading: Planning the cost of a new well near Ponderosa Park
sections.html:
For Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock in this area, the drilling model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the local median depth of 360 feet, that puts the drilled hole at about $18,000 to $25,200. A finished system, including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, is modeled at approximately $24,000 to $37,200.

Treat those figures as a budgeting range, not a fixed quote. A bid can change with the final depth, casing and grout requirements, difficult access, water-level conditions, pump size, trench length, power availability, and the location of the house. Ask the contractor to separate drilling, casing, grouting, development, pump equipment, electrical, trenching, testing, and permit-related work so you can compare bids on the same scope.

sections.heading: Environmental, septic, and building checks before you buy
sections.html:
Mapped environmental records within about ten miles include 24 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 2 historic mine features, and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That does not establish contamination at a particular parcel, but it is a reason to check the exact location, drainage, prior land use, and available water-quality results. Test the existing well for routine drinking-water concerns and any contaminants suggested by local site history.

Low yield is not the main warning in these records, but dry holes and variable fractured-bedrock conditions remain possible. Confirm casing, grout, wellhead protection, pump performance, and separation from septic components. Before building, have the county and a qualified septic designer review soils, setbacks, reserve area, driveway access, and the proposed house location. Water quantity, water quality, legal use, and septic approval are separate questions.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Ponderosa Park?
faq.a: Ponderosa Park wells have a median reported depth of 360 feet. The middle half runs from 300 to 434 feet, and 65% are between 300 and 600 feet. About 11% exceed 600 feet, while the deepest recorded well is 2,318 feet. A nearby well is useful evidence, but the target aquifer and exact geology still control the final depth.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Ponderosa Park?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 360-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $18,000 to $25,200. A completed system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is estimated at $24,000 to $37,200. Access, depth, casing, grout, pump requirements, and trench length can change the quote.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Ponderosa Park?
faq.a: Reported wells have a median pump yield of 13.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. About 72% produce 5 to 15 gallons per minute and 27% exceed 15 gallons per minute. These are reported pump yields, not a promise for a new well or unrestricted water use.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Ponderosa Park?
faq.a: The regional records include 24 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about ten miles, along with 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That does not prove a specific well is unsafe. Test the property’s water, review its history and nearby environmental sites, and inspect the wellhead and septic separation before relying on it for household drinking water.
